introduction-engineering-is-a-gamble.core: Every deploy, design choice or ignored debt ticket is a bet. Risk modelling makes those bets explicit so you can manage them instead of discovering them in an incident.

first_principles.problem: Teams either ignore risk until it bites or freeze in fear of it. Neither is engineering. Drivers don't refuse to drive; they use seatbelts, mirrors and insurance.
derivation: Make each bet **explicit**: what could go wrong?
Spend mitigation effort where the **expected loss** is highest.

analogy.title: Driving on the motorway
analogy.story: You accept a small chance of an accident every time you merge, and manage it with seatbelts, speed and insurance.
analogy.breaks: Traffic risks are well studied. System risks must be discovered by your own team.

example.title: Skipping a failover test
example.scenario: A team keeps postponing its DR test.

steps.label: Explicit
steps.detail: "Untested failover" goes in the risk register.

steps.label: Act
steps.detail: It scores high, so a test is scheduled this quarter.

example.outcome: a hidden bet becomes a managed risk.

check.q: Why is ignoring risk different from accepting it?
check.a: Accepting is a conscious, recorded choice; ignoring means you don't know what you're exposed to.

the-risk-formula-likelihood-impact.core: Risk = likelihood × impact. Score the two separately, because a frequent small failure and a rare catastrophe need different responses.

first_principles.problem: Teams prioritise by gut or by the scariest-sounding item. A meteor strike and a full disk both sound bad, but one happens monthly.
truths: Likelihood is a probability in a time window.
Impact is cost when it happens (users, money, trust).
derivation: Estimate **likelihood** per period (once a month, once in 5 years).
Estimate **impact** in concrete terms ($, users, hours).
Look at both factors too: rare catastrophes may need special handling.

analogy.title: Home insurance
analogy.story: Insurers price policies by how often fires happen in your area times how much your house costs to rebuild.
analogy.breaks: Insurers have actuarial data. Engineers usually estimate, so use ranges and revisit.

example.title: Disk full vs region outage
example.outcome: spending matches real exposure, not fear.

check.q: Why score likelihood and impact separately?
check.a: Frequent small failures and rare huge ones have similar scores but need different responses.

risk-registers-your-living-inventory-of-.core: A risk register lists every known risk with likelihood, impact, score, mitigation, gap, owner and review date, turning knowledge in people's heads into a shared, trackable inventory.

first_principles.problem: Risk knowledge lives with individual engineers; when they leave or go on holiday, it evaporates, and the same risks surprise the team again.
truths: You can't manage what isn't written down.
Risks without owners don't get mitigated.
derivation: Columns: **ID, description, likelihood, impact, score, mitigation, gap, owner, last reviewed**.

analogy.title: A home maintenance list
analogy.story: "Roof tiles loose, gutter blocked, boiler due a service", each with a date and who's handling it.
analogy.breaks: House issues are visible. System risks are often invisible until written down.

example.title: R-001: untested DB failover

steps.label: Gap
steps.detail: The mitigation exists on paper but isn't proven.

steps.label: Action
steps.detail: The owner schedules a failover drill.

example.outcome: the team's risks are visible, owned and reviewed.

check.a: To show what's still missing between current mitigation and acceptable risk.

value-at-risk-var-in-engineering-terms.core: Value at Risk translates technical risk into money: expected incident frequency × cost per incident (lost revenue, recovery effort, penalties). Executives understand dollars, not MTTR.

first_principles.problem: "Our failover is untested" doesn't get budget. "We carry $40,000 a year of unmitigated exposure" does.
derivation: Estimate **cost per incident**: revenue/hour × duration + people cost + penalties + churn.

analogy.title: A financial portfolio's VaR
analogy.story: Banks state how much they could lose on a bad day with 95% confidence. Engineering VaR states what a bad outage could cost.
analogy.breaks: Market data is plentiful. Incident costs are estimates, so present ranges.

example.title: Database outage VaR

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: A $30k HA setup is clearly worth it.

example.outcome: risk work is funded because it's expressed in business terms.

check.a: Executives understand money; it lets them compare risk reduction with other investments.

risk-matrices-and-heat-maps.core: A risk matrix plots risks on 5×5 likelihood and impact scales and colours the cells, so priorities are obvious at a glance to technical and non-technical people.

first_principles.problem: A long list of risks hides which ones matter. Stakeholders need to see the dangerous corner instantly.
derivation: Define **5-point scales** with concrete meanings (likelihood: rare → weekly; impact: negligible → catastrophic).

analogy.title: A weather map
analogy.story: Red zones show where storms are severe and likely. You check the red first.
analogy.breaks: Weather maps are measured. Risk scores are judgements, so calibrate scales with examples.

example.title: Quarterly risk review

steps.label: Red
steps.detail: Untested backups, single-AZ DB, expiring certs.

steps.label: Action
steps.detail: Owners and dates for each red item.

example.outcome: leadership sees in one slide where risk reduction is needed.

check.q: Why define concrete meanings for each rating?
check.a: So different people score consistently instead of by feel.

the-four-risk-response-strategies.core: Every risk gets one of four responses: avoid it, mitigate it, transfer it, or accept it. Know which you're choosing and why.

first_principles.problem: Without named strategies, risks either get ignored (accidental acceptance) or over-engineered. 'We'll deal with it' isn't a strategy.
truths: Some risks can be removed entirely.
Some can be paid for by others; some aren't worth fixing.
derivation: **Avoid**: don't do the risky thing (use proven Postgres instead of a new DB).
**Transfer**: shift to someone else (managed service, insurance, SLA).

analogy.title: Travel risks
analogy.story: Avoid: don't travel. Mitigate: lock your bag. Transfer: buy travel insurance. Accept: you might get rained on.
analogy.breaks: Insurance pays out cleanly. Transferring to a vendor still leaves you with customer impact.

example.title: Four risks, four responses
example.scenario: A platform team reviews its register.

steps.label: Accept
steps.detail: Low-impact internal tool: documented acceptance with review date.

example.outcome: every risk has a deliberate, recorded response.

check.q: Does transferring a risk remove it?
check.a: Not entirely: the vendor handles the failure, but your customers can still be affected.

failure-mode-and-effects-analysis-fmea-f.core: FMEA walks through every component asking how it can fail, what happens when it does, and how you'd detect it, then scores severity × occurrence × detection to find hidden risks.

first_principles.problem: Brainstorming finds the obvious risks. The ones that hurt are often silent failures nobody would notice until damage is done.
truths: Every component can fail in several ways.
Undetected failures do the most damage.
derivation: Score **severity, occurrence, detection** (1–10) → **RPN** = S × O × D.
Fix the highest RPN, especially poor detection.

analogy.title: A pre-flight checklist
analogy.story: Pilots check each system for how it could fail and how they'd notice, not just the ones that failed last time.
analogy.breaks: Aircraft designs are stable. Systems change weekly, so FMEAs need refreshing.

example.title: FMEA on a backup job

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Severity high and detection poor: worst combination.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Alert if no successful backup in 26 hours.

example.outcome: a silent killer gets an alarm.

check.q: What does FMEA add beyond likelihood × impact?
check.a: Detectability: how likely you are to notice the failure before it causes damage.

preparing-for-black-swans.core: Black swans are unpredictable, extreme events explained only in hindsight. You can't forecast them, but you can build resilience: redundancy, isolation, recoverability and practised response.

first_principles.problem: Risk models only cover what you can imagine. A provider losing your data, a supply-chain compromise or a global outage can still happen.
truths: Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence.
Recovery ability helps against any failure.
derivation: Avoid **single points of failure** you can't live without.

analogy.title: Black swans in Australia
analogy.story: Europeans were certain all swans were white, until 1697. Confidence came from limited observation.
analogy.breaks: Swans are harmless. Black-swan outages can end companies, so invest in recovery even without forecasts.

example.title: Cloud account compromised
example.scenario: An attacker deletes production and backups in the same account.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.detail: Backups in a separate, locked-down account with object lock.

example.outcome: even unforeseeable events leave you a way back.

check.q: Why focus on recoverability instead of prediction?
check.a: Recovery works for any failure, including ones nobody imagined.
